numbers.reconciliation: Jobs: about 9.8 million fewer exist in 2040 than there would have been; the biggest remover is software doing tasks, the biggest offset cheaper output selling more. People: over the period about 11.7 million found the job they had, or would have had, gone: 8.1 million positions never offered to new entrants, 3.0 million layoffs, 366,000 full-time equivalents of gig and freelance hours cut. Of them, 9.4 million found other work, 1.1 million left the workforce and 197,000 are unemployed in 2040. The two ledgers differ because someone who finds other work fills a position that would otherwise have gone to someone else: the jobs ledger counts positions, the people ledger counts people.

beats.title: More jobs than today, fewer than there would have been
beats.sentence: There are about 152.4 million jobs today. Without further AI progress, population and normal growth would take that to about 174.2 million by 2040. With AI the model's median is about 164.4 million (about 8% more than today; likely between 155.3 million and 173.9 million): about 9.8 million fewer than there would have been, one job in 18 removed. The biggest remover is software doing tasks; the biggest offset is cheaper output selling more.
beats.range: Likely between 18.8 million fewer and 253,000 fewer than there would have been; against today, between 2% more and 14% more.
beats.what_changes_it: How much of the productivity gain gets spent back into the economy. Spent back, jobs are flat or up against the no-AI path; pocketed, the loss doubles.

beats.title: Most of the gap is hiring that never happens; about one position in 4 removed is a layoff
beats.sentence: Of the 11.5 million positions AI takes out of the economy by 2040 in the central run, 8.1 million are jobs never offered to new entrants and 3.0 million are layoffs. Unemployment rises by at most 458,000 at its 2037 peak. Of the people affected, 9.4 million find other work and 1.1 million leave the workforce. Reality check: employers announced 54,836 AI-cited job cuts in 2025 (model: 67,668) and 173,568 AI-cited job cuts since 2023 through June 2026 (model: 143,034), by Challenger, Gray & Christmas's count. The baseline's layoff pace is fitted to these counts: a quarter of each required cut is taken as layoffs at once rather than waiting for attrition. The counts are announcements, which include positions closed by attrition and redeployment, so the fit is deliberately loose; without it the model's attrition-first rule produced a tenth of the announced layoffs. If employers cut through layoffs twice as readily (the layoffs-first variant): 1.8 million layoffs by 2030 and 3.8 million by 2040 instead of 3.0 million, unemployment peaking 563,000 above the no-AI path, and total jobs about the same: the same gap, borne by incumbents instead of entrants.
beats.range: Hiring-first holds in every scenario the model ships; the layoff share is fitted to 2025–2026 announcements and is the least certain number here.
beats.what_changes_it: How fast employers cut ahead of attrition: the attrition rate and the layoff pace, both levers in the technical brief. Faster cuts do not change the total; they move it from entrants to incumbents and raise the unemployment peak.

beats.title: The young pay first
beats.sentence: Workers under 25 carry 34% of the shortfall, about 4% of their group's jobs, against 1% for 25 to 44 and 1% for those over 55. Workers without a degree lose 3 times as much as graduates, and the bottom half of earners lose about 2% of their jobs while the top tenth is barely affected.
beats.range: Incumbents are mostly safe; entrants are not. That is the practical advice hidden in the numbers.
beats.what_changes_it: Whether employers cut through attrition (which lands on entrants) or through layoffs (which lands on incumbents).

beats.title: Pay goes up, the worker's share goes down
beats.sentence: Real pay is about 4% higher by 2040 (roughly $2,494 a year for a $60,000 earner) because prices fall about 4%. The economy is about 8% larger. But workers' share of national income falls by 4.8 points: the gains are real and they go disproportionately to owners.
beats.what_changes_it: How much of the cost saving reaches prices; if firms keep it as margin, pay rises less and the owner share rises more.

beats.title: Three waves, not one
beats.sentence: Office and analytical work is being reshaped now: graphic designers (-17%), network and computer systems administrators (-8%), computer user support specialists (-8%), computer occupations, all other (-8%) by 2030. Robots and vehicles arrive later: 0.2% of task-hours in 2030, 6.9% by 2040. AI-made content takes translation and voice first (72% of spending by 2040) and video last (8%). Growing: sales and related workers, all other (+11%), production workers, all other (+11%), nursing assistants (+7%), dental hygienists (+6%).
beats.range: Timing of the robot wave depends on how fast fleets can be built and approved, not on the software.
beats.what_changes_it: Production ramps, permits, and hardware costs for the robot wave; how much people keep paying for human-made work for the content wave.

beats.title: The money flows to the U.S. and the chip makers
beats.sentence: By 2040 US collects about $151 billion a year in AI income; CN $50 billion, EU $35 billion, TW $26 billion. The largest GDP gains are in TW, KR (chip exports); the largest job losses in UK, EU. That income is paid by employers replacing tasks with software (84% of the $282 billion spent on AI worldwide in 2040), employers buying tools that speed up workers (11%), and consumers paying for AI-made content (6%); the work being bought is mostly management ($42 billion), business & financial ($34 billion), office & admin support ($33 billion). It lands with the cloud and data-centre operators ($54 billion), the model makers ($47 billion), the chip makers ($38 billion).
beats.range: Regional splits rest on where models, data centres and chips are made; the country-level job numbers outside the U.S. use placeholder occupation mixes.
beats.what_changes_it: Data-localization rules, export controls, and where the next fabs and data centres are built.

beats.title: Two futures, and the difference is partly a choice
beats.sentence: Gains spent back: If productivity gains are spent back into the economy, employment in 2040 is +13% versus no AI (about 23.1 million more jobs). Gains pocketed: If the gains are saved or paid out as rents, employment is -6% (about 10.2 million fewer jobs). Preset: Seba / RethinkX disruption: With Seba / RethinkX disruption assumptions, employment in 2040 is -7% and robots and vehicles do 9% of task-hours; robotaxis pass 10% of driver work in 2030. Preset: Seba / RethinkX 2026 (humanoids and TaaS): With Seba / RethinkX 2026 (humanoids and TaaS) assumptions, employment in 2040 is -8% and robots and vehicles do 11% of task-hours; robotaxis pass 10% of driver work in 2030.
beats.range: The model's biggest uncertainty is whether the gains are spent back into the economy or pocketed; that is partly policy, partly corporate behaviour, and partly what people choose to pay for.
beats.what_changes_it: See the futures and the policy runs below.

policies.name: retraining subsidy 50% of wage
policies.sentence: retraining subsidy 50% of wage: no measurable change in total jobs, 38,000 fewer unemployed; costs about $5 billion a year, of which the deficit carries $5 billion. Pays half the wage of workers who enrol in retraining, so more of the displaced retrain and more complete it; paid from the deficit.

policies.name: wage insurance 50% for 2 years
policies.sentence: wage insurance 50% for 2 years: no measurable change in total jobs; costs about $3 billion a year. Tops up the pay of displaced workers who take a lower-paid job, half the gap for two years; paid from a tax on AI spending.

policies.name: $500/month basic income, AI-tax financed
policies.validity_note: deficit-financed transfers above 3% of GDP are outside the model's validity: it has no inflation or interest-rate response, so their demand effect is overstated
policies.sentence: $500/month basic income, AI-tax financed: 14.2 million more jobs than the baseline by 2040, 71,000 more unemployed; costs about $1742 billion a year, of which the deficit carries $1721 billion. Pays every adult $500 a month; a 30% tax on AI spending covers a small part and the deficit the rest. A deficit this large is outside what the model can judge: it has no inflation or interest-rate response, so the jobs effect is overstated.

policies.name: 36-hour standard week
policies.sentence: 36-hour standard week: 18.4 million more jobs than the baseline by 2040, real pay per head -10.5 points. Shortens the standard week to 36 hours, so the same work is shared among more people; pay per head falls in step and total pay does not.

paragraphs: The money going in. The four largest cloud companies spent about $413 billion on data centres, chips and power in 2025 and have guided to about $732 billion for 2026. The model takes that path as given: $720 billion in 2026, rising to $1.1 trillion a year by 2030 and flat after, about $15.6 trillion over 2024–2040.

The money coming back to AI producers. In the model, employers and consumers spend $21 billion a year on AI in 2026, $155 billion by 2030 and $260 billion by 2040: $2.7 trillion over the period, 17% of the capital spent. Producers' cumulative revenue never catches up with cumulative capex by 2040. This is revenue for replacing and speeding up work and for AI-made content, priced at what the tokens cost; it is not the whole AI industry's sales (consumer subscriptions, advertising, search, coding assistants used as experiments, and internal use are outside the model).

The return to the economy. The same AI adds about $1.5 trillion a year of productivity gain by 2030 and $4.2 trillion by 2040 across the modelled regions ($36.0 trillion cumulative, 2.3 times the capital spent; the productivity gain alone repays the capex by 2032). Counting the data-centre build itself as output, the GDP effect is $4.5 trillion a year by 2040. Most of that gain goes to the firms that adopt AI and, through lower prices, to their customers, not to the companies that built the capacity.

How the two fit together. The investment is a bet that revenue will grow into the capacity: the capex path is front-loaded and the model's revenue follows adoption, so by construction the first years look like a bubble on a revenue-to-capex basis. Three things can close the gap: AI revenue far above what labour substitution alone justifies (consumer and advertising businesses, or prices held well above token cost); adoption faster than the model's central pace (the Seba presets are that case); or investors accepting that, as with railways, electricity and fibre, society earns most of the return and the builders earn a normal or poor one. The model cannot say which; it can say that the productivity return is real and large, that it lands with adopters, and that it arrives a decade after the capital.

investment.definition: AI producers' revenue (called AI rents by value-chain stage in the technical documents) is what the makers of models, the cloud and data-centre operators, the chip makers and the integrators receive: in the model it is exactly what employers and consumers spend on AI, split across those four stages and allocated to the regions whose companies hold the market share. It is gross revenue, not profit and not economic rent in the textbook sense.

glossary.versus no AI: compared with a world in which AI stopped improving in 2023; population and normal growth are the same in both
glossary.likely range: the middle 80% of the model's runs; one run in ten falls above it and one in ten below
glossary.we would bet on it / leaning / a coin fl: how sure the model is of the direction: sure across all its versions, mostly, or split
glossary.AI income (AI producers' revenue): what the makers of models, the cloud and data-centre operators, the chip makers and the integrators receive; in the model this equals what employers and consumers spend on AI, split by stage and allocated to the regions whose companies hold the market share; gross revenue, not profit and not economic rent in the textbook sense
glossary.jobs today: employment in the 831 modelled occupations plus self-employed and platform workers, in full-time equivalents; about 152 million in 2024 against the 158 million BLS total
glossary.jobs ledger / people ledger: positions that exist versus people whose job was affected; a person who finds other work takes a position someone else would have had, so the two do not add up to each other
